tools.name: configuration_view
tools.description: Get the current Kubernetes configuration content as a kubeconfig YAML

minified.description: Return a minified version of the configuration. If set to true, keeps only the current-context and the relevant pieces of the configuration for that context. If set to false, all contexts, clusters, auth-infos, and users are returned in the configuration. (Optional, default true)

tools.name: events_list
tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). Supported fields: involvedObject.kind, involvedObject.name, involvedObject.namespace, involvedObject.uid, involvedObject.apiVersion, involvedObject.resourceVersion, involvedObject.fieldPath, reason, reportingComponent, source, type. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the events from. If not provided, will list events from all namespaces

tools.name: kiali_get_logs
tools.description: Get the logs of a Kubernetes Pod (or workload name that will be resolved to a pod) in a namespace. Output is plain text, matching kubernetes-mcp-server pods_log. The line_count field tells you the total number of log lines returned. Analyze ALL of them, but summarize the results unless the user explicitly asks for the raw output. Do not omit any error or warning lines.

container.description: Optional. Name of the Pod container to get the logs from.

format.description: Output formatting for chat. 'codeblock' wraps logs in ~~~ fences (recommended). 'plain' returns raw text like kubernetes-mcp-server pods_log.

meshCluster.description: Optional Istio mesh cluster name from kiali_list_mesh_clusters (e.g. west). When omitted, Kiali defaults to its home cluster.

name.description: Name of the Pod to get the logs from. If it does not exist, it will be treated as a workload name and a running pod will be selected.

namespace.description: Namespace to get the Pod logs from

previous.description: Optional. Return previous terminated container logs

severity.description: Optional severity filter applied client-side. Accepts 'ERROR', 'WARN' or combinations like 'ERROR,WARN'.

tail.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, defaults to 50). Cannot exceed 200 lines.

workload.description: Optional. Workload name override (used when name lookup fails).

tools.name: kiali_get_mesh_status
tools.description: Retrieves the high-level health, topology, and environment details of the Istio service mesh. Returns multi-cluster control plane status (istiod), data plane namespace health (including ambient mesh status), observability stack health (Prometheus, Grafana...), and component connectivity. Use this tool as the first step to diagnose mesh-wide issues, verify Istio/Kiali versions, or check overall health before drilling into specific workloads.

tools.name: kiali_get_mesh_traffic_graph
tools.description: Returns service-to-service traffic topology, dependencies, and network metrics (throughput, response time, mTLS) for the specified namespaces. Use this to diagnose routing issues, latency, or find upstream/downstream dependencies.

graphType.description: Granularity of the graph. 'app' aggregates by app name, 'versionedApp' separates by versions, 'workload' maps specific pods/deployments. Default: versionedApp.

meshCluster.description: Optional Istio mesh cluster name from kiali_list_mesh_clusters (e.g. west). When omitted, Kiali defaults to its home cluster.

namespaces.description: Comma-separated list of namespaces to map

tools.name: kiali_get_metrics
tools.description: Returns a compact JSON summary of Istio metrics (latency quantiles, traffic trends, throughput, payload sizes) for the given resource.

byLabels.description: Comma-separated list of labels to group metrics by (e.g., 'source_workload,destination_service'). Optional

meshCluster.description: Optional Istio mesh cluster name from kiali_list_mesh_clusters (e.g. west). When omitted, Kiali defaults to its home cluster.

quantiles.description: Comma-separated list of quantiles for histogram metrics (e.g., '0.5,0.95,0.99'). Optional

rateInterval.description: Rate interval for metrics (e.g., '1m', '5m'). Optional, defaults to '10m'

reporter.description: Metrics reporter(s). Comma-separated list of: 'source', 'destination', 'waypoint', or the special value 'both' (no reporter filter). Optional, defaults to 'source'. Example: 'source,waypoint'

resourceName.description: Name of the resource to get metrics for

resourceType.description: Type of resource to get metrics

step.description: Step between data points in seconds (e.g., '15'). Optional, defaults to 15 seconds

tools.name: kiali_get_pod_performance
tools.description: Returns a human-readable text summary with current Pod CPU/memory usage (from Prometheus) compared to Kubernetes requests/limits (from the Pod spec). Useful to answer questions like 'Is this workload using too much memory?'

meshCluster.description: Optional Istio mesh cluster name from kiali_list_mesh_clusters (e.g. west). When omitted, Kiali defaults to its home cluster.

podName.description: Kubernetes Pod name. If workloadName is provided, the tool will attempt to resolve a Pod from that workload first.

queryTime.description: Optional end timestamp (RFC3339) for the query. Defaults to now.

timeRange.description: Time window used to compute CPU rate (Prometheus duration like '5m', '10m', '1h', '1d'). Defaults to '10m'.

workloadName.description: Kubernetes Workload name (e.g. Deployment/StatefulSet/etc). Tool will look up the workload and pick one of its Pods. If not found, it will fall back to treating this value as a podName.

tools.name: kiali_get_resource_details
tools.description: Fetches a list of resources OR retrieves detailed data for a specific resource. If 'resourceName' is omitted, it returns a list. If 'resourceName' is provided, it returns details for that specific resource.

meshCluster.description: Optional Istio mesh cluster name from kiali_list_mesh_clusters (e.g. west). When omitted, Kiali defaults to its home cluster.

namespaces.description: Comma-separated list of namespaces to query (e.g., 'bookinfo' or 'bookinfo,default'). If not provided, it will query across all accessible namespaces.

resourceName.description: Optional. The specific name of the resource. If left empty, the tool returns a list of all resources of the specified type. If provided, the tool returns deep details for this specific resource.

resourceType.description: The type of resource to query. Use 'app' for Kiali applications (grouped by the Kubernetes 'app' label). Use 'argoapp' for ArgoCD Application CRDs (requires ArgoCD installed and the Kiali service account must have read permissions on applications.argoproj.io).

tools.name: kiali_get_trace_details
tools.description: Fetches a single distributed trace by trace_id and returns its call hierarchy (service tree with duration, status, and nested calls). Use this after list_traces to drill into a specific trace.

traceId.description: Trace ID to fetch and summarize. If provided, namespace/service_name are ignored.

tools.name: kiali_list_mesh_clusters
tools.description: Returns the list of Istio mesh clusters that Kiali can access. Each entry includes its name and whether it is the home cluster (where Kiali is deployed). Call this tool before using meshCluster on other Kiali tools when the target cluster is unknown.

tools.name: kiali_list_traces
tools.description: Lists distributed traces for a service in a namespace. Returns a summary (namespace, service, total_found, avg_duration_ms) and a list of traces with id, duration_ms, spans_count, root_op, slowest_service, has_errors. Use get_trace_details with a trace id to get full hierarchy.

errorOnly.description: If true, only consider traces that contain errors. Default false.

limit.description: Maximum number of traces to return. Default 10.

lookbackSeconds.description: How far back to search. Default 600 (10m).

meshCluster.description: Optional Istio mesh cluster name from kiali_list_mesh_clusters (e.g. west). When omitted, Kiali defaults to its home cluster.

serviceName.description: Service name to search traces for (required). Returns multiple traces up to limit.

tools.name: kiali_manage_istio_config
tools.description: Create, patch, or delete Istio, Gateway API, and Inference API config. Supports Istio resources (networking.istio.io, security.istio.io), Gateway API resources (gateway.networking.k8s.io), and Inference API resources (inference.networking.k8s.io) when installed on the cluster. For list and get (read-only) use manage_istio_config_read.

data.description: JSON or YAML data for the resource. Required for create and patch actions. For create, you can provide partial content (e.g. only spec) and it will be merged onto a valid template with defaults. Arrays (like servers, http, etc.) are REPLACED entirely, so include ALL elements you want.

group.description: API group of the Istio object. Use 'gateway.networking.k8s.io' for Gateway API resources. Use 'inference.networking.k8s.io' for Inference API resources.

meshCluster.description: Optional Istio mesh cluster name from kiali_list_mesh_clusters (e.g. west). When omitted, Kiali defaults to its home cluster.

version.description: API version. Use 'v1' for all resource types.

tools.name: kiali_manage_istio_config_read
tools.description: Read Istio, Gateway API, and Inference API config. 'list' groups by namespace→'group/version/kind'→{valid:[...],invalid:[...]} where valid/invalid arrays contain resource names; omit group/kind to retrieve ALL config types in a single call. Supports Istio (networking.istio.io, security.istio.io), Gateway API (gateway.networking.k8s.io), and Inference API (inference.networking.k8s.io) when installed. 'get' returns full YAML. For writes use manage_istio_config.

group.description: API group of the Istio object. Required ONLY for 'get' action. For 'list', OMIT group and kind to retrieve ALL config types in a single call. Use 'gateway.networking.k8s.io' for Gateway API resources. Use 'inference.networking.k8s.io' for Inference API resources.

kind.description: Kind of the Istio object. Required ONLY for 'get' action. For 'list', OMIT to return all kinds at once — do NOT call separately for each kind.

meshCluster.description: Optional Istio mesh cluster name from kiali_list_mesh_clusters (e.g. west). When omitted, Kiali defaults to its home cluster.

namespace.description: Namespace containing the Istio object. For 'list', if not provided, returns objects across all namespaces. For 'get', required.

object.description: Name of the Istio object. Required for 'get' action.

serviceName.description: Filter Istio configurations (VirtualServices, DestinationRules, and their referenced Gateways) that affect a specific service. Only applicable for 'list' action

version.description: API version. Use 'v1' for all resource types. Required for 'get' action.

tools.name: namespaces_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes namespaces in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter namespaces by field values (e.g. 'metadata.name=default', 'status.phase=Active'). Supported fields: metadata.name, status.phase. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

tools.name: nodes_log
tools.description: Get logs from a Kubernetes node (kubelet, kube-proxy, or other system logs). This accesses node logs through the Kubernetes API proxy to the kubelet

name.description: Name of the node to get logs from

query.description: query specifies services(s) or files from which to return logs (required). Example: "kubelet" to fetch kubelet logs, "/<log-file-name>" to fetch a specific log file from the node (e.g., "/var/log/kubelet.log" or "/var/log/kube-proxy.log")

tailLines.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, 0 means all logs)

tools.name: nodes_stats_summary
tools.description: Get detailed resource usage statistics from a Kubernetes node via the kubelet's Summary API. Provides comprehensive metrics including CPU, memory, filesystem, and network usage at the node, pod, and container levels. On systems with cgroup v2 and kernel 4.20+, also includes PSI (Pressure Stall Information) metrics that show resource pressure for CPU, memory, and I/O. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/understand-psi-metrics/ for details on PSI metrics

name.description: Name of the node to get stats from

tools.name: nodes_top
tools.description: List the resource consumption (CPU and memory) as recorded by the Kubernetes Metrics Server for the specified Kubernetes Nodes or all nodes in the cluster

label_selector.description: Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'node-role.kubernetes.io/worker=') to filter nodes by label (Optional, only applicable when name is not provided)

name.description: Name of the Node to get the resource consumption from (Optional, all Nodes if not provided)

tools.name: pods_delete
tools.description: Delete a Kubernetes Pod in the current or provided namespace with the provided name

name.description: Name of the Pod to delete

namespace.description: Namespace to delete the Pod from

tools.name: pods_exec
tools.description: Execute a command in a Kubernetes Pod (shell access, run commands in container) in the current or provided namespace with the provided name and command

command.description: Command to execute in the Pod container. The first item is the command to be run, and the rest are the arguments to that command. Example: ["ls", "-l", "/tmp"]

container.description: Name of the Pod container where the command will be executed (Optional)

name.description: Name of the Pod where the command will be executed

namespace.description: Namespace of the Pod where the command will be executed

tools.name: pods_get
tools.description: Get a Kubernetes Pod in the current or provided namespace with the provided name

namespace.description: Namespace to get the Pod from

tools.name: pods_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes pods in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter pods by field values (e.g. 'status.phase=Running', 'spec.nodeName=node1'). Supported fields: metadata.name, metadata.namespace, spec.nodeName, spec.restartPolicy, spec.schedulerName, spec.serviceAccountName, status.phase (Pending/Running/Succeeded/Failed/Unknown), status.podIP, status.nominatedNodeName. Note: CrashLoopBackOff is a container state, not a pod phase, so it cannot be filtered directly. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

labelSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'app=myapp,env=prod' or 'app in (myapp,yourapp)'), use this option when you want to filter the pods by label

tools.name: pods_list_in_namespace
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes pods in the specified namespace in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter pods by field values (e.g. 'status.phase=Running', 'spec.nodeName=node1'). Supported fields: metadata.name, metadata.namespace, spec.nodeName, spec.restartPolicy, spec.schedulerName, spec.serviceAccountName, status.phase (Pending/Running/Succeeded/Failed/Unknown), status.podIP, status.nominatedNodeName. Note: CrashLoopBackOff is a container state, not a pod phase, so it cannot be filtered directly. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

labelSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'app=myapp,env=prod' or 'app in (myapp,yourapp)'), use this option when you want to filter the pods by label

tools.name: pods_log
tools.description: Get the logs of a Kubernetes Pod in the current or provided namespace with the provided name

container.description: Name of the Pod container to get the logs from (Optional)

name.description: Name of the Pod to get the logs from

namespace.description: Namespace to get the Pod logs from

tail.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, default: 100)

tools.name: pods_run
tools.description: Run a Kubernetes Pod in the current or provided namespace with the provided container image and optional name

image.description: Container Image to run in the Pod

name.description: Name of the Pod (Optional, random name if not provided)

namespace.description: Namespace to run the Pod in

port.description: TCP/IP port to expose from the Pod container (Optional, no port exposed if not provided)

tools.name: pods_top
tools.description: List the resource consumption (CPU and memory) as recorded by the Kubernetes Metrics Server for the specified Kubernetes Pods in the all namespaces, the provided namespace, or the current namespace

all_namespaces.description: If true, list the resource consumption for all Pods in all namespaces. If false, list the resource consumption for Pods in the provided namespace or the current namespace

label_selector.description: Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'app=myapp,env=prod' or 'app in (myapp,yourapp)'), use this option when you want to filter the pods by label (Optional, only applicable when name is not provided)

name.description: Name of the Pod to get the resource consumption from (Optional, all Pods in the namespace if not provided)

namespace.description: Namespace to get the Pods resource consumption from (Optional, current namespace if not provided and all_namespaces is false)

tools.name: projects_list
tools.description: List all the OpenShift projects in the current cluster

tools.name: resources_create_or_update
tools.description:
Create or update a Kubernetes resource via Server-Side Apply. The manifest is the complete desired state: any field this tool previously set and the new manifest omits is removed. To edit an existing resource, fetch it with resources_get, modify it, then re-apply the full resource.
(common apiVersion and kind include: v1 Pod, v1 Service, v1 Node, apps/v1 Deployment, networking.k8s.io/v1 Ingress, route.openshift.io/v1 Route)

resource.description: Complete YAML or JSON representation of the Kubernetes resource (full desired state, not a partial patch). Include apiVersion, kind, metadata, and the full spec.

tools.name: resources_delete
tools.description:
Delete a Kubernetes resource in the current cluster by providing its apiVersion, kind, optionally the namespace, and its name
(common apiVersion and kind include: v1 Pod, v1 Service, v1 Node, apps/v1 Deployment, networking.k8s.io/v1 Ingress, route.openshift.io/v1 Route)

apiVersion.description: apiVersion of the resource (examples of valid apiVersion are: v1, apps/v1, networking.k8s.io/v1)

gracePeriodSeconds.description: Optional duration in seconds before the object should be deleted. Value must be non-negative integer. The value zero indicates delete immediately. If this value is nil, the default grace period for the specified type will be used

kind.description: kind of the resource (examples of valid kind are: Pod, Service, Deployment, Ingress)

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to delete the namespaced resource from (ignored in case of cluster scoped resources). If not provided, will delete resource from configured namespace

tools.name: resources_get
tools.description:
Get a Kubernetes resource in the current cluster by providing its apiVersion, kind, optionally the namespace, and its name
(common apiVersion and kind include: v1 Pod, v1 Service, v1 Node, apps/v1 Deployment, networking.k8s.io/v1 Ingress, route.openshift.io/v1 Route)

apiVersion.description: apiVersion of the resource (examples of valid apiVersion are: v1, apps/v1, networking.k8s.io/v1)

kind.description: kind of the resource (examples of valid kind are: Pod, Service, Deployment, Ingress)

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the namespaced resource from (ignored in case of cluster scoped resources). If not provided, will get resource from configured namespace

tools.name: resources_list
tools.description:
List Kubernetes resources and objects in the current cluster by providing their apiVersion and kind and optionally the namespace and label selector
(common apiVersion and kind include: v1 Pod, v1 Service, v1 Node, apps/v1 Deployment, networking.k8s.io/v1 Ingress, route.openshift.io/v1 Route)

apiVersion.description: apiVersion of the resources (examples of valid apiVersion are: v1, apps/v1, networking.k8s.io/v1)

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter resources by field values (e.g. 'status.phase=Running', 'metadata.name=myresource'). Supported fields vary by resource type. For Pods: metadata.name, metadata.namespace, spec.nodeName, spec.restartPolicy, spec.schedulerName, spec.serviceAccountName, status.phase (Pending/Running/Succeeded/Failed/Unknown), status.podIP, status.nominatedNodeName. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

kind.description: kind of the resources (examples of valid kind are: Pod, Service, Deployment, Ingress)

labelSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'app=myapp,env=prod' or 'app in (myapp,yourapp)'), use this option when you want to filter the resources by label

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the namespaced resources from (ignored in case of cluster scoped resources). If not provided, will list resources from all namespaces

tools.name: resources_scale
tools.description: Get or update the scale of a Kubernetes resource in the current cluster by providing its apiVersion, kind, name, and optionally the namespace. If the scale is set in the tool call, the scale will be updated to that value. Always returns the current scale of the resource

apiVersion.description: apiVersion of the resource (examples of valid apiVersion are apps/v1)

kind.description: kind of the resource (examples of valid kind are: StatefulSet, Deployment)

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to get/update the namespaced resource scale from (ignored in case of cluster scoped resources). If not provided, will get/update resource scale from configured namespace

scale.description: Optional scale to update the resources scale to. If not provided, will return the current scale of the resource, and not update it

outputSteps.content:
Done. Here’s what I set up and verified:

- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1 in namespace canary-deployment-ns
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine with containerPort 80 and the same (default/empty) security configuration as the stable deployment
- Updated Service recommendation-engine
  - Selector changed from app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine so it targets both v2.0 and v2.1 pods
  - Ports unchanged (port 80 -> targetPort 8080) to match the existing stable setup

Verification
- Pods:
  - engine-v2-0: 2/2 Running
  - engine-v2-1: 2/2 Running
- Service endpoints now include 4 backends (2 from v2.0 and 2 from v2.1), so traffic will be approximately 50/50 based on equal endpoint count.

Notes and how to adjust
- To shift the split, scale one of the deployments. For example, scaling canary to 3 and stable to 1 yields ~75/25 canary/stable.
- To immediately revert to stable-only, set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0, or scale canary to 0 replicas, or delete engine-v2-1.

If you want an exact weighted split independent of replica counts, we can set that up via an Ingress/Gateway or a service mesh rule.

Root cause
- The Deployment overridden the nginx entrypoint with: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, which fails. Pod logs: "/bin/sh: 1: nonexistent_command: not found". This caused back-off restarts.

What I changed
- Replaced the Deployment to remove the invalid command/args so it uses the default nginx-unprivileged entrypoint.
- Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
- Exposed containerPort 8080 (nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 by default).

- New Pod is running and ready:

I fixed it. Summary:

- Root cause: The pod requested PVC homepage-pvc with storageClass sc, but that StorageClass doesn’t exist. The scheduler kept the pod Pending with “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims.”

  - Recreated it with a valid StorageClass: standard (the cluster’s default).
- Result:
  - PVC homepage-pvc is Bound (1Gi, RWO).
  - Pod homepage-pod is now Running on node mcp-eval-cluster; container is Ready with 0 restarts.

- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod -o wide
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pvc homepage-pvc

outputSteps.content:
I fixed it. Summary:

- Root cause: The pod requested PVC homepage-pvc with storageClass sc, but that StorageClass doesn’t exist. The scheduler kept the pod Pending with “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims.”
- What I changed:
  - Deleted the stuck PVC homepage-pvc (it had never bound, so no data was lost).
  - Recreated it with a valid StorageClass: standard (the cluster’s default).
- Result:
  - PVC homepage-pvc is Bound (1Gi, RWO).
  - Pod homepage-pod is now Running on node mcp-eval-cluster; container is Ready with 0 restarts.

If you intended a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or a different size/access mode, tell me and I’ll adjust the PVC accordingly. To double-check locally:
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod -o wide
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pvc homepage-pvc

Want me to expose this pod via a Service so you can reach it?

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but your Deployment’s probes were checking port 80 (/get_status and /is_ready), causing liveness/readiness failures and restarts.
- The Service was also targeting port 80, so cluster traffic couldn’t reach the app.

What I changed
- Deployment (orders/webapp):
  - Probes now check / on port 8080:
    - readinessProbe: GET / on 8080 (initialDelaySeconds 2, periodSeconds 5)
    - livenessProbe: GET / on 8080 (initialDelaySeconds 10, periodSeconds 10)
    - startupProbe: GET / on 8080 (failureThreshold 30, periodSeconds 1)
  - Declared a named container port http on 8080 (kept 80 as secondary; safe but unused).
- Service (orders/webapp):
  - Updated targetPort to the named port http (maps to container port 8080).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: 1/1 Ready.
- Deployment is Available with 1 replica.
- Service endpoints now point to 10.244.0.38:8080.
- Basic in-pod check to 127.0.0.1:8080 succeeded.

How to verify
- In-cluster:
  - kubectl -n orders run -it --rm curl --image=curlimages/curl:8.9.1 -- sh -lc 'curl -sSI http://webapp/orders || curl -sSI http://webapp'
- From your workstation via port-forward:
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - Then browse http://localhost:8080

Optional next steps
- If you need external access, I can create an Ingress or LoadBalancer Service.
- If your app is supposed to expose custom health endpoints, tell me the correct paths/ports and I’ll adjust the probes accordingly.

namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but your Deployment’s probes were checking port 80 (/get_status and /is_ready), causing liveness/readiness failures and restarts.
- The Service was also targeting port 80, so cluster traffic couldn’t reach the app.

What I changed
- Deployment (orders/webapp):
  - Probes now check / on port 8080:
    - readinessProbe: GET / on 8080 (initialDelaySeconds 2, periodSeconds 5)
    - livenessProbe: GET / on 8080 (initialDelaySeconds 10, periodSeconds 10)
    - startupProbe: GET / on 8080 (failureThreshold 30, periodSeconds 1)
  - Declared a named container port http on 8080 (kept 80 as secondary; safe but unused).
- Service (orders/webapp):
  - Updated targetPort to the named port http (maps to container port 8080).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: 1/1 Ready.
- Deployment is Available with 1 replica.
- Service endpoints now point to 10.244.0.38:8080.
- Basic in-pod check to 127.0.0.1:8080 succeeded.

How to verify
- In-cluster:
  - kubectl -n orders run -it --rm curl --image=curlimages/curl:8.9.1 -- sh -lc 'curl -sSI http://webapp/orders || curl -sSI http://webapp'
- From your workstation via port-forward:
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - Then browse http://localhost:8080

Optional next steps
- If you need external access, I can create an Ingress or LoadBalancer Service.
- If your app is supposed to expose custom health endpoints, tell me the correct paths/ports and I’ll adjust the probes accordingly.

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but your Deployment’s probes were checking port 80 (/get_status and /is_ready), causing liveness/readiness failures and restarts.
- The Service was also targeting port 80, so cluster traffic couldn’t reach the app.

What I changed
- Deployment (orders/webapp):
  - Probes now check / on port 8080:
    - readinessProbe: GET / on 8080 (initialDelaySeconds 2, periodSeconds 5)
    - livenessProbe: GET / on 8080 (initialDelaySeconds 10, periodSeconds 10)
    - startupProbe: GET / on 8080 (failureThreshold 30, periodSeconds 1)
  - Declared a named container port http on 8080 (kept 80 as secondary; safe but unused).
- Service (orders/webapp):
  - Updated targetPort to the named port http (maps to container port 8080).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: 1/1 Ready.
- Deployment is Available with 1 replica.
- Service endpoints now point to 10.244.0.38:8080.
- Basic in-pod check to 127.0.0.1:8080 succeeded.

How to verify
- In-cluster:
  - kubectl -n orders run -it --rm curl --image=curlimages/curl:8.9.1 -- sh -lc 'curl -sSI http://webapp/orders || curl -sSI http://webapp'
- From your workstation via port-forward:
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - Then browse http://localhost:8080

Optional next steps
- If you need external access, I can create an Ingress or LoadBalancer Service.
- If your app is supposed to expose custom health endpoints, tell me the correct paths/ports and I’ll adjust the probes accordingly.

Summary of findings
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pod labels:
  - Service selector: app=web
  - Pod/Deployment labels: app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so it couldn’t route traffic.
- The nginx container listens on port 8080, not 80.
  - Even after fixing the selector, targetPort was 80, so traffic still failed.

What I changed (applied to the cluster)
1) Fixed the selector on Service web/nginx to match the Pod label:
   - spec.selector: app=nginx
2) Corrected the Service port mapping:
   - spec.ports[0].port: 80
   - spec.ports[0].targetPort: 8080

Verification
- Created a temporary test pod (nettool) in namespace web and:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local → 200 (OK)
  - Direct curl to the Pod IP showed 8080 returns 200, confirming the app listens on 8080.

Current state
- Service web/nginx (ClusterIP 10.97.165.156) is healthy and accessible inside the cluster on port 80.
- It routes correctly to the nginx Pod on container port 8080.

Notes/next steps
- If you need external access (from outside the cluster), this Service is type ClusterIP, which is internal-only. I can:
  - Switch it to type LoadBalancer or NodePort, or
  - Create an Ingress/Gateway to expose it with a hostname/TLS.
- I can remove the temporary nettool pod I used for testing. Would you like me to delete it now?

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Summary of findings
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pod labels:
  - Service selector: app=web
  - Pod/Deployment labels: app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so it couldn’t route traffic.
- The nginx container listens on port 8080, not 80.
  - Even after fixing the selector, targetPort was 80, so traffic still failed.

What I changed (applied to the cluster)
1) Fixed the selector on Service web/nginx to match the Pod label:
   - spec.selector: app=nginx
2) Corrected the Service port mapping:
   - spec.ports[0].port: 80
   - spec.ports[0].targetPort: 8080

Verification
- Created a temporary test pod (nettool) in namespace web and:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local → 200 (OK)
  - Direct curl to the Pod IP showed 8080 returns 200, confirming the app listens on 8080.

Current state
- Service web/nginx (ClusterIP 10.97.165.156) is healthy and accessible inside the cluster on port 80.
- It routes correctly to the nginx Pod on container port 8080.

Notes/next steps
- If you need external access (from outside the cluster), this Service is type ClusterIP, which is internal-only. I can:
  - Switch it to type LoadBalancer or NodePort, or
  - Create an Ingress/Gateway to expose it with a hostname/TLS.
- I can remove the temporary nettool pod I used for testing. Would you like me to delete it now?

Summary of findings
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pod labels:
  - Service selector: app=web
  - Pod/Deployment labels: app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so it couldn’t route traffic.
- The nginx container listens on port 8080, not 80.
  - Even after fixing the selector, targetPort was 80, so traffic still failed.

What I changed (applied to the cluster)
1) Fixed the selector on Service web/nginx to match the Pod label:
   - spec.selector: app=nginx
2) Corrected the Service port mapping:
   - spec.ports[0].port: 80
   - spec.ports[0].targetPort: 8080

Verification
- Created a temporary test pod (nettool) in namespace web and:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local → 200 (OK)
  - Direct curl to the Pod IP showed 8080 returns 200, confirming the app listens on 8080.

Current state
- Service web/nginx (ClusterIP 10.97.165.156) is healthy and accessible inside the cluster on port 80.
- It routes correctly to the nginx Pod on container port 8080.

Notes/next steps
- If you need external access (from outside the cluster), this Service is type ClusterIP, which is internal-only. I can:
  - Switch it to type LoadBalancer or NodePort, or
  - Create an Ingress/Gateway to expose it with a hostname/TLS.
- I can remove the temporary nettool pod I used for testing. Would you like me to delete it now?

results.taskOutput:
Summary of findings
- Root cause: Your Deployment had a nodeSelector set: environment=production-gpu. The only node in the cluster does not have that label, so the scheduler could not place any pods. Events showed FailedScheduling: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.” With no pods running/ready, the Service had no endpoints, so calls to web-app-service resulted in connection refused.
- Service/selector looked correct (selector app=web-app), but there were no ready endpoints when the pods were Pending.

What I changed
- Removed the conflicting nodeSelector from the web-app-deployment so the pods can schedule on the available node.
- Ensured the container exposes port 80 and added basic readiness/liveness probes on port 80 to guard against routing to unready pods.

Current state
- Deployment web-app-deployment is Available with 2/2 replicas Ready.
- Service web-app-service now has 2 ready endpoints:
  - 10.244.0.43
  - 10.244.0.44
- One additional pod briefly showed as not ready during the rollout and is being drained by the controller; traffic won’t be sent to it because it’s not in the ready endpoints.

How to validate
- From any pod in the cluster:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run tmp-curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- sh -c "curl -sS http://web-app-service"
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service
- From the cluster:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get deploy,po,svc
  - You should see deploy ready 2/2, pods 1/1 ready, and service endpoints listed.

Notes/next steps
- If you intended to restrict this to specific nodes (e.g., GPU nodes), either:
  - Re-add an appropriate nodeSelector/tolerations AND label the nodes, for example:
    - kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
  - Or use a workload-specific nodeSelector/affinity that matches labels actually present in your cluster.
- If you want me to reintroduce scheduling constraints safely (and keep the app running), tell me which node labels you plan to use and I can update the manifest accordingly.

Summary of findings
- Root cause: Your Deployment had a nodeSelector set: environment=production-gpu. The only node in the cluster does not have that label, so the scheduler could not place any pods. Events showed FailedScheduling: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.” With no pods running/ready, the Service had no endpoints, so calls to web-app-service resulted in connection refused.
- Service/selector looked correct (selector app=web-app), but there were no ready endpoints when the pods were Pending.

What I changed
- Removed the conflicting nodeSelector from the web-app-deployment so the pods can schedule on the available node.
- Ensured the container exposes port 80 and added basic readiness/liveness probes on port 80 to guard against routing to unready pods.

Current state
- Deployment web-app-deployment is Available with 2/2 replicas Ready.
- Service web-app-service now has 2 ready endpoints:
  - 10.244.0.43
  - 10.244.0.44
- One additional pod briefly showed as not ready during the rollout and is being drained by the controller; traffic won’t be sent to it because it’s not in the ready endpoints.

How to validate
- From any pod in the cluster:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run tmp-curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- sh -c "curl -sS http://web-app-service"
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service
- From the cluster:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get deploy,po,svc
  - You should see deploy ready 2/2, pods 1/1 ready, and service endpoints listed.

Notes/next steps
- If you intended to restrict this to specific nodes (e.g., GPU nodes), either:
  - Re-add an appropriate nodeSelector/tolerations AND label the nodes, for example:
    - kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
  - Or use a workload-specific nodeSelector/affinity that matches labels actually present in your cluster.
- If you want me to reintroduce scheduling constraints safely (and keep the app running), tell me which node labels you plan to use and I can update the manifest accordingly.

outputSteps.content:
Summary of findings
- Root cause: Your Deployment had a nodeSelector set: environment=production-gpu. The only node in the cluster does not have that label, so the scheduler could not place any pods. Events showed FailedScheduling: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.” With no pods running/ready, the Service had no endpoints, so calls to web-app-service resulted in connection refused.
- Service/selector looked correct (selector app=web-app), but there were no ready endpoints when the pods were Pending.

What I changed
- Removed the conflicting nodeSelector from the web-app-deployment so the pods can schedule on the available node.
- Ensured the container exposes port 80 and added basic readiness/liveness probes on port 80 to guard against routing to unready pods.

Current state
- Deployment web-app-deployment is Available with 2/2 replicas Ready.
- Service web-app-service now has 2 ready endpoints:
  - 10.244.0.43
  - 10.244.0.44
- One additional pod briefly showed as not ready during the rollout and is being drained by the controller; traffic won’t be sent to it because it’s not in the ready endpoints.

How to validate
- From any pod in the cluster:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run tmp-curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- sh -c "curl -sS http://web-app-service"
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service
- From the cluster:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get deploy,po,svc
  - You should see deploy ready 2/2, pods 1/1 ready, and service endpoints listed.

Notes/next steps
- If you intended to restrict this to specific nodes (e.g., GPU nodes), either:
  - Re-add an appropriate nodeSelector/tolerations AND label the nodes, for example:
    - kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
  - Or use a workload-specific nodeSelector/affinity that matches labels actually present in your cluster.
- If you want me to reintroduce scheduling constraints safely (and keep the app running), tell me which node labels you plan to use and I can update the manifest accordingly.

Next step (needed to see 3Gi inside the pod)
- Restart storage-pod so the kubelet can finish the filesystem resize on mount. This will cause brief downtime since storage-pod is a standalone Pod (not managed by a Deployment).

Do you want me to:
- delete and recreate storage-pod now to complete the resize?

outputSteps.content:
I’ve resized the PVC used by storage-pod to 3Gi.

What I changed
- PVC resize-pv/storage-pvc requests: 3Gi (was 1Gi)
- StorageClass csi-hostpath-sc allows expansion
- PV now shows capacity: 3Gi

Current status
- PVC status shows FileSystemResizePending: Kubernetes indicates the filesystem resize will complete when the pod remounts the volume.
- This CSI driver requires a pod restart to finalize the filesystem growth inside the container.

Next step (needed to see 3Gi inside the pod)
- Restart storage-pod so the kubelet can finish the filesystem resize on mount. This will cause brief downtime since storage-pod is a standalone Pod (not managed by a Deployment).

Do you want me to:
- delete and recreate storage-pod now to complete the resize?

Done. I upgraded the rollout-test/web-app Deployment to image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.25 and adjusted the rollout strategy to avoid downtime.

What I changed
- Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.25
- Rolling update strategy: maxUnavailable: 0 (kept maxSurge: 25%) to ensure at least the original number of replicas stayed available during the rollout.

Status/verification
- Deployment web-app is at revision 2 with 3/3 pods updated and available.
- All pods are running the new ReplicaSet (web-app-6b6947d6cf) and are Ready 1/1.
- Events show a clean surge-and-drain rollout: scaled up new RS, then gradually scaled down old RS; no warnings/errors observed.

Notes
- Setting maxUnavailable: 0 prevents capacity dips during future rollouts but briefly increases pod count (by up to 25% here). If you prefer to revert to the previous 25% unavailability for future updates, say the word.
- For even safer zero-downtime rollouts, consider adding a readinessProbe and a short preStop hook to allow in-flight requests to drain before termination.

Want me to keep this zero-downtime strategy as the default on this Deployment going forward?

  name: db

kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: db
  namespace: statefulset-test
spec:
  serviceName: db
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: db
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: init-volume
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
        args:
          - |
            set -e
            if [ ! -f /data/test ]; then
              echo -n "initial_data" > /data/test
            fi
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
      containers:
      - name: main
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["/bin/sh","-c","sleep infinity"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: data
    spec:
      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 1Gi

Summary of findings

- Workload/pod state:
  - Found productpage-v1 pod running (2/2 containers) in bookinfo.
  - productpage container logs show only Gunicorn startup; no application errors.
  - istio-proxy sidecar logs (last 200 lines) show successful 200 responses for /productpage and its downstream calls (/details, /reviews); no 500s observed in the recent tail.

- Istio config (bookinfo namespace):
  - There are two VirtualServices affecting productpage:
    - bookinfo (normal gateway routing to productpage:9080)
    - productpage-fault (additional VS)
  - productpage-fault VirtualService details:
    - hosts: productpage, productpage.bookinfo.svc.cluster.local, productpage-bookinfo.apps-crc.testing
    - http:
      - route → destination.host: productpage
      - fault.abort.httpStatus: 500
      - fault.abort.percentage.value: 100
    - Kiali warning: “More than one Virtual Service for same host”
  - This config injects a fault that aborts requests with HTTP 500 at 100% for traffic targeting productpage (from mesh sidecars, and it even declares the external host name).

Most likely root cause

- An intentional Istio fault injection rule is configured in the productpage-fault VirtualService to always return HTTP 500 responses. This explains 500s without any application errors in productpage logs.

Recommended next steps

- Disable or remove the fault injection:
  - Option A: delete the test VirtualService:
    - kubectl delete virtualservice productpage-fault -n bookinfo
  - Option B: patch to set fault.abort.percentage.value: 0 or remove the fault block.
- After change, re-test the productpage endpoint. If issues persist, we can also check the ingress gateway logs, but the fault VS is the clear cause here.

Steps.message:
Summary of findings

- Workload/pod state:
  - Found productpage-v1 pod running (2/2 containers) in bookinfo.
  - productpage container logs show only Gunicorn startup; no application errors.
  - istio-proxy sidecar logs (last 200 lines) show successful 200 responses for /productpage and its downstream calls (/details, /reviews); no 500s observed in the recent tail.

- Istio config (bookinfo namespace):
  - There are two VirtualServices affecting productpage:
    - bookinfo (normal gateway routing to productpage:9080)
    - productpage-fault (additional VS)
  - productpage-fault VirtualService details:
    - hosts: productpage, productpage.bookinfo.svc.cluster.local, productpage-bookinfo.apps-crc.testing
    - http:
      - route → destination.host: productpage
      - fault.abort.httpStatus: 500
      - fault.abort.percentage.value: 100
    - Kiali warning: “More than one Virtual Service for same host”
  - This config injects a fault that aborts requests with HTTP 500 at 100% for traffic targeting productpage (from mesh sidecars, and it even declares the external host name).

Most likely root cause

- An intentional Istio fault injection rule is configured in the productpage-fault VirtualService to always return HTTP 500 responses. This explains 500s without any application errors in productpage logs.

Recommended next steps

- Disable or remove the fault injection:
  - Option A: delete the test VirtualService:
    - kubectl delete virtualservice productpage-fault -n bookinfo
  - Option B: patch to set fault.abort.percentage.value: 0 or remove the fault block.
- After change, re-test the productpage endpoint. If issues persist, we can also check the ingress gateway logs, but the fault VS is the clear cause here.

outputSteps.content:
Here’s what I found.

Where time is spent (distributed traces)
- productpage → reviews → ratings path is the hotspot.
- Several slow traces (~10,023–10,030 ms total) show:
  - Slowest service: reviews.bookinfo (~10,009 ms).
  - Inside reviews, the outbound call to ratings.bookinfo.svc.cluster.local dominates:
    - ratings call spans are ~10,008–10,010 ms with http.status_code=0 (timeout/cancel), indicating the client gave up waiting.
  - Example traces: 6783e21124de1dc9c63273ce4221173e, 7b2c3213f575aad1d8fbbe892f6495df, 806cca44ecbc1caff8a0b84dd26ba874.
- productpage also makes fast calls to details; those complete in ~1–2 ms and aren’t contributing.

Istio config that applies to this path
- VirtualService bookinfo (routes /productpage and related paths at the gateway to productpage:9080). No faults/timeouts here; just basic routing.
- VirtualService ratings (applies to ratings traffic):
  - hosts: ratings.bookinfo.svc.cluster.local
  - http:
    - route → destination host ratings.bookinfo.svc.cluster.local, subset v1
    - fault:
      - delay: fixedDelay 25s
      - percentage: 100%
- DestinationRule ratings:
  - host: ratings.bookinfo.svc.cluster.local
  - subsets: v1 (labels: version=v1)

Relating mesh config to the observed delay
- The ratings VirtualService injects a 25s delay on 100% of requests.
- The traces show the reviews → ratings call stalls ~10s and then ends with http.status_code=0, which is consistent with an upstream application or Envoy timeout (~10s) expiring before the injected 25s delay completes.
- As a result, reviews spends ~10s waiting on ratings and then either times out or falls back (reviews spans sometimes return 200 while the nested ratings span shows status 0), which pushes overall productpage latency to ~10s despite the final HTTP 200.

Most likely root cause
- Intentional fault injection on ratings via the ratings VirtualService:
  - fault.delay fixedDelay=25s at 100% of traffic causes the reviews → ratings call to exceed client/sidecar timeouts (~10s), creating the productpage latency spike.

Suggested next steps (quick wins)
- Remove or reduce the ratings VirtualService fault delay (or lower its percentage), or explicitly set shorter per-route timeouts/fallbacks if you’re testing resilience.
- If the delay is intentional for testing, confine it to a subset or a smaller traffic percentage to avoid cluster-wide latency impacts.
